nameStory: Watercress gets its name from its preferred home in clear, flowing water - 'cress' comes from an old Germanic word meaning 'to creep or crawl,' describing how this plant spreads along stream beds. The 'water' part is obvious once you see it thriving in brooks and springs where few other plants dare to grow.
description: Watercress is a low-growing, sprawling plant that loves to have its feet wet in clean, flowing water. It forms dense mats of bright green, compound leaves that float on or emerge from shallow streams and springs. The plant rarely grows more than a foot tall, instead spreading horizontally along the water's surface with hollow, succulent stems that can root at the nodes where they touch mud or stones.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 3-9 rounded leaflets arranged like a feather along the stem, with the terminal leaflet being the largest. The leaves feel crisp and succulent, with a distinctly peppery, watercress-sandwich taste when nibbled (if you're sure of your identification and the water is clean).

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms floating or semi-submerged mats in shallow, flowing water with hollow, pale green stems that feel spongy when squeezed. The stems root easily wherever they touch soil or sediment.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white flowers with four petals arranged in small clusters at the stem tips, appearing from late spring through fall. Each flower is only about 1/8 inch across but they're numerous enough to create a subtle white sparkle over the green mat.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, curved seed pods (siliques) that look like tiny curved swords, containing two rows of seeds. The pods are about half an inch long and feel slightly bumpy when rolled between your fingers.

habitat: Look for watercress in clean, cool, slow-moving streams, springs, and the shallow edges of ponds throughout New England. It thrives in alkaline water with a steady flow and often grows alongside wild mint and monkey flower. You'll rarely find it in stagnant water or polluted streams.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges bright green from overwintering roots, and the plant begins its rapid spread across water surfaces. Early white flowers may appear by late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with lush green mats covering suitable waterways. White flowers bloom continuously, and the peppery taste is at its mildest and most pleasant.
seasonality.fall: Continues flowering and growing until hard frost, though leaves may become more peppery and tough. Seeds ripen in their curved pods throughout the season.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to roots in most of New England, though in protected springs with flowing water, some green growth may persist under ice.

funFact: Watercress has been eaten by humans for over 3,000 years and was considered so nutritious that ancient Greek soldiers ate it to boost their strength - it contains more vitamin C than oranges and more iron than spinach!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other small aquatic plants like water speedwell or brooklime, but watercress is the only one with compound leaves that have that distinctive peppery bite. Remember: compound leaves + peppery taste + flowing water = watercress.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse this edible watercress with the ornamental nasturtium flowers often called 'watercress' in garden centers - they're completely different plants! Also, only harvest watercress from clean water sources, as it can concentrate pollutants and may harbor parasites in contaminated water.
compareHints: Narrow-fruited watercress, the only close relative in New England, has more deeply divided leaflets and narrower seed pods, but the differences are subtle. Both share the same peppery taste and aquatic habitat, making them nearly impossible to distinguish without close examination of the seed pods.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Narrow-fruited watercress differs from regular watercress mainly in its seed pods, which are much thinner and more curved rather than short and plump.
